rationale: JevLite (open Qwen3-4B LoRA typed readout, 3-seed ensemble) reached AUROC .974 on 577 held-out turn decisions, non-inferior to the MiniMax-M3 LLM judge at the pre-registered .02 margin (+.027 [-.011, .065]) and not significantly better than a ModernBERT encoder, with ECE .052 vs .054, 100% vs 82.3% on legitimate calls, and a gray/legit deficit (38.1% vs 50.0%, n=3 scenarios) the authors place within seed noise; recipe was selected with test-set exposure and callers are synthetic (Sec. 5, Table 2, Table 3).

Used zero-shot to estimate whether other LLMs' answers are correct, Jev reached AUROC 0.666 [0.638, 0.691] on 1,718 text responses (above verbalized-confidence baselines 0.610-0.649 and a GPT-5-mini judge 0.532, far below the trained PINOCCHIO 0.868) but ECE 0.133, worse than recalibrated baselines (0.009-0.034) and the LLM judge (0.110), and the authors conclude it gives no usable correctness signal off the shelf (Table 3; App. E.10).

Model rankings by baseline accuracy and by correctness across 12 repeated request conditions diverge: Jev had the lowest hosted baseline accuracy (77.38% vs 78.96-83.21%) but kept 23/30 anchors correct in all 12 responses (second to Claude Sonnet 5's 24; difference one target), with 5 anchors repeated wrong throughout, so agreement alone does not establish correctness (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2-4.3).

On 123 ContractNLI test contracts (2,091 judgments) Jev had 77.38% [75.99, 78.81] accuracy, below all seven hosted LLMs (78.96-83.21%; paired gap significant vs Gemini Flash-Lite +5.16 pp [3.49, 6.98] but not vs GPT-5.6 Luna [-0.05, 3.11]), at the lowest cost ($0.000228/contract) and median latency (1.24 s) (Table 1, Sec. 4.1).

In an emulated 10,000-seat enterprise built from 46 synthetic scenarios (109 turns) and public session corpora, Jev-labelled cache-safe routing recovered 13.4% of model spend ($3.3M/yr) vs 20.8% with perfect labels, with per-axis classifier accuracy 63-82% and author-only ground-truth tags; Jev is not self-hostable, so a self-hosted encoder is the stated fallback (Table 3, Sec. 4.6, Sec. 5.1, Sec. 8).

The router moves a turn only when Jev's per-option probabilities clear 0.80 and otherwise holds it, which held 42% of routable turns in place while 12.5% of moved turns were still false downgrades; savings depend on this hold rule and on unvalidated author tags (Table 3, Fig. 4, Sec. 8).

Exploratory single runs with and without a Jev decision layer against one 13-vulnerability target: the Jev run hit 9/13 seeded scenarios vs 10/13 for the LLM-only run, reported 18 vs 16 findings, recalibrated 9 severities and finished 5 min 19 s faster, but the author states the runs lack statistical power and the severity comparison comes from a re-test with a changed harness (Sec. IX, Tables VI-VIII).

LAVOIR (open Laya-based ModernBERT encoder) is statistically indistinguishable from the Bayes ceiling on seen schemas and a Gini cap stops it asking when confident, but out-of-distribution calibration is weak (ABCD ECE 0.19), it is wrong on 19% of ABCD cases where its confidence is at least 0.99, and zero-shot schemas reach only 0.51-0.52 vs a 0.667 ceiling (Sec. 7.1-7.2, Limitations).

With at most 0.5 questions per conversation the ask-or-decide policy is 14.1 points more accurate than never asking and matches a greedy oracle (AUC 0.799 vs 0.797), and on real ABCD dialogues one exchange adds 8.3 [4.9, 11.7] points where it asks and none where it does not, but the 19% error rate at confidence >= 0.99 means acting when confident still passes confident errors (Sec. 7.1-7.2).

On 812 typed questions (9,744 single-edit variants), one unverified observer opinion appended to the state flipped 12.1% [8.5, 15.5] of decisions (+11.1 pp over re-run noise), statistically tied with the strongest injected command (10.1%), at least one of nine delivered attacks flipped 29.2% of questions, and 88.8% of multi-option targeted flips landed on the attacker's option (Table 2, Sec. 4.2-4.3).

A 0.8 confidence gate let 12.6% [7.5, 20.3] of attack flips through (24.1% for observer opinion) while already routing 18.7% of clean answers to review, the opinion pushed 38.0% of confident answers below the gate (+37.5 pp over re-run), and Noul answers carry no confidence, so the gate catches most flips but not all and floods review (Sec. 4.4).

Independent preregistered study: the released Laya Typed-Decisions checkpoint was uniformly under-confident (signed gap -0.214); one disjointly fitted temperature cut held-out ECE from 0.204 to 0.037, but the frozen selection rule picked an overfitting isotonic calibrator and H2 failed on both tracks (Abstract, Sec. 4.2, Sec. 6).

The frozen confidence gate beat random escalation at matched rate (Delta +0.0646 [0.0502, 0.0785], H3b supported) but missed its 10% accepted-set error target out of sample on both tracks (0.140 and 0.103, H3a failed), accepted confidence-1.0 security errors, and case-level gating fell to 5.5% coverage (Sec. 7, Sec. 8.1).

Across ten SemEval corpora in six languages, frozen Jev plus 488 CPU-fitted coefficients gave the lowest aggregate Task-1 RMSE (1.0645, an untested 0.0018 below the next team), but raw scores reached only 2.0731, it trailed the best published score on 8 of 10 corpora, and extraction beat fine-tuned Llama-3.3-70B and GPT-OSS-120B baselines but trailed a generative retrieval-and-rules system by about 4 points and was weakest on Chinese laptop (Sec. 4.2-4.4, Tables 2-4).

On 1,800 class-balanced accelerometer windows (5,400 decisions) Jev's probabilities were poorly calibrated: ECE 0.10-0.50 across nine dataset-representation cells (best representation 0.253, 0.349, 0.129) with mean maximum probability 0.37/0.58/0.30 against argmax accuracy 0.11/0.24/0.17, and 86 vectors failed validity; the generative Claude baseline returned no probabilities (Table 3, Sec. 4).

Over 288,000 VSM-2013 answers, Jev without a persona answered like its own American personas (0.08 on an American-to-Saudi scale in English, 0.06 in Arabic), reproduced 87% of the human Saudi-US difference in English but 62% in Arabic with long-term orientation reversed, and shifted profiles in stereotyped ways by age and gender, in all eight request designs (Abstract, Fig. 1, Sec. 4.7).

Jev's confidence was lower in Arabic and for Saudi personas and followed the language of the framing rather than of the items; the authors note this could flag answers resting on less evidence but cannot show calibration because value items have no correct answer (Sec. 4.6, Sec. 5.4).

Used as a stand-in for survey respondents, Jev defaults to an American value profile, captures only 62% of the human Saudi-US difference in Arabic, and mis-ranks 33% of dimensions with no matched profile having all six in order, so simulated publics lean to one culture (Sec. 4.8, Sec. 5.3).

On the authors' own CJ-Bench, the open Chinese-Jev (initialised from Laya Multilingual) reached 69.20% vs hosted Jev 68.35% on general Chinese decisions and 87.65% vs 84.29% on medical, but trailed Jev on legal (60.10 vs 68.35) and finance (64.72 vs 78.39), 92% of Jev's average; both typed models far exceeded the generative Qwen3.5-2B baseline (32.95% general) (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2).

Chinese-Jev General had ECE 3.78% vs hosted Jev 11.45% and Qwen3.5-2B 43.68% on general tasks, but after domain fine-tuning the specialists' average ECE (12.08%) exceeded Jev's (5.57%) and rose on legal (15.37% to 17.45%) (Tables 1-2, Sec. 4.2).

With Qwen3-1.7B over 3 seeds, two-stage RLCD matched GRPO+TS accuracy on GSM8K-Verify (92.2% vs 91.8%) with far better selective prediction (AURC 0.034 vs 0.061; 81.1% vs 19.4% of items decidable at 5% error), beat all reasoning baselines on MMLU-Pro (+5.3 points over SFT+TS), and on annotator-disagreement ChaosNLI matched rather than beat cross-entropy (JSD 0.075 vs 0.074) (Table 1, Table 3, Sec. 5).

After tuning a Jev prompt separately for each dataset, held-out ECE was 0.027 on 3,066 WiC pairs and 0.025 on 612 ChaosNLI stories with most bins within sampling error, but the author says the tuning step is critical (untuned scores bear no relation to ground truth) and top bins understate the true rate, making it less suited to high-confidence uses (Methodology, Results, Conclusion).

Opinion post: because Jev returns only a floating-point number with no justification, the content signals behind a decision cannot be inspected and hidden bias is hard to detect, so bias should be a primary concern (e.g. ranking job applicants); a single informal 'Good city?' probe is anecdotal (section 'Black boxes are back in fashion').

On 200 ZebraLogic puzzles, showing GPT-5.6 Luna Jev's probabilities during revision added nothing beyond a Jev-triggered plain second look (43.0% vs 44.5% without reasoning; 97.0% vs 97.0% at high effort) and on flagged items fixed 3 answers but broke 6, so Jev's number worked as a trigger but did not inform the revision (Sec. 6.2, Table 4).

As an escalation trigger Jev flagged 93% of Luna's no-reasoning errors at 92% precision but only 70% at 8.5% precision once Luna used high-effort reasoning, and Jev-triggered second looks added 3.5 and 2.0 points; replacing Luna's answer on disagreement changed one correct high-effort answer to wrong (Sec. 6.1-6.3, Tables 4-5).

As a candidate checker Jev was 5-60 points more accurate than GPT-5.6 Luna without reasoning (e.g. sparse ordering 98.3% vs 85.0%) and matched reasoning-enabled Luna on two moderate logic sets at about one-fifth to one-sixth of the cost, but fell below it on sparse ordering (98.3% vs 100%) and the hardest set (4/5 vs 5/5) (Tables 2-3, Sec. 6.4).

Archived AI-assisted dialogue (ChatGPT, Perplexity responses) arguing that Jev's guarantee is syntactic and that typed inference can relocate ontology-governance commitments into schemas, rubrics, thresholds and compute graphs that are less visible and less contestable; no measurement (full PDF read).

On identical 500-600-item samples of seven public moderation, hallucination, NLI and injection tasks, Jev had the highest AUROC of the cheap-tier LLMs on all six binary tasks (0.90-0.99), tied Claude Haiku 4.5 on ANLI, and was never significantly worse than a cheap-tier model, though frontier Claude Sonnet 4.6 (42-97x the cost) beat it on ANLI-R3 and HaluEval-Dialogue; full-split re-runs (54,634 decisions) stayed within the sample CIs (Tables 2-3, Table 12, Sec. 6).

The study does not attack Jev itself: it shows Jev detecting prompt injection as a task (AUROC 0.994 on 500 items and on the full 2,060-item split), while packing eight short items into one call lowered injection AUROC by 0.018 as adjacent adversarial items appeared to bleed into one another (Tables 2, 12; Sec. 3.3).

Jev's raw probabilities had the lowest mean Brier of all systems (0.103 vs 0.116-0.159 for five LLMs) and after cross-fitted Platt recalibration stayed better than the cheap tier and GPT-5.4 (0.076 vs 0.101-0.130) but not Claude Sonnet 4.6 (0.071); raw ECE 0.104 was similar to Haiku's 0.101 and one paraphrase raised BoolQ ECE to 0.30 (Table 8, Sec. 4, Sec. 7).

Escalating Jev's uncertain band to an LLM rarely helped (2 of 30 cascades significant, both via Sonnet 4.6) because LLM accuracy inside the band was 0.21-0.85, so the author recommends routing that band to a human; Jev's own risk-coverage curves were monotone (98.6% accuracy at 80% coverage on ToxicChat) (Sec. 4-5, Tables 10-11).

Technical note proposing a Decision Orchestration Layer in which a decision below a validated confidence threshold escalates to a more capable model and high-risk decisions go to a human, stressing that thresholds must be measured on labelled workflow data; no measurement (Sec. 12, Sec. 17).

On 270 policy-derived authorization cases x 3 repetitions, Jev's permission Brier was lower than GPT-4.1 mini's (0.0263 vs 0.0555; difference -0.0292 [-0.0557, -0.0070]) with 6 vs 13 tier-only false allows, but not distinguishable from DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (0.0267 vs 0.0337, interval includes zero), and Jev denied 18/357 reference-hold attempts vs 1-2 for the comparators; labels come from an author-written oracle without human adjudication (Tables III-IV, Sec. V).

A fixed probability gate removed Jev's 6 false allows but withheld 29 additional correct allows (298 vs 327 of 345), a development-selected gate kept zero false allows at 320/345, the gate left GPT-4.1 mini's 13 false allows unchanged, and DeepSeek reached zero false allows with more correct allows (315 vs 295) (Table III, Sec. V-D, V-E).

Full text shows no typed decision model is measured: Bajev is a deterministic Kleene three-valued rule engine (threshold, keyword and hashing-embedding agents) that scored 100/100 with zero false certainty on an author-written corpus plus 105 unit tests, and 'JEV' appears only in its name; recorded empirical=no so it is excluded from typed-model tallies (Sec. 4-5, Sec. 10).

Per-node rule traceability (threshold, evidence and rule recorded for every verdict, conflicts quarantined to U) is demonstrated for a deterministic rule engine, not for any typed decision model; recorded empirical=no so it is excluded from typed-model tallies (Sec. 2, Sec. 6-7, Sec. 13).

Eliciting bilateral truth tuples on ten constructed items, Jev (5 repeats) declared the liar sentence Order-0 like gpt-4o-mini and deepseek-chat but with the weakest margin (T+F 1.01-1.04), turned unambiguous facts into order 1 through noise in one probe, and like the LLMs did not reach designed intermediate orders; its outputs varied from call to call (Sec. 3.3, Sec. 4, Table 2).

On 300 authored allow/hold/deny cases (one session per model), Jev's 28 errors concentrated on hold references (9 allowed and 16 denied of 111), 10 of them at selected probability >= 0.9 (our count from the workbook), KEV-4B erred similarly and the open CLM v0.1-8B held all 300 cases, while Jev's correctness AUROC (0.82) exceeded the self-reported GLM 5.3 FlashX (0.73) (RESULTS-SUMMARY; workbook Results sheet).

Jev 1.13.0 decided 272/300 cases correctly (90.67% [86.8, 93.5]) and the open KEV-4B 273/300, both above the generative GLM 5.3 FlashX (260/300; Jev minus GLM +4.00 pp [0.33, 7.34], GLM losing 33 truncated outputs), while the open CLM v0.1-8B scored 111/300 by returning hold throughout (RESULTS-SUMMARY tables).

On 7,081 author-generated held-out Polish decisions hosted Jev scored 0.780 and English-oriented open typed models 0.59-0.78 (losing 13-23 points relative to English), while the Polish-trained open basal-1.0-4.5B reached 0.884; it tied Jev on 1,479 held-out English decisions (0.741 vs 0.736) but trailed it on public JevBench (0.740 vs 0.861), so closing the language gap required language-specific training (Table 23, Sec. 20).

With a confidence threshold fixed on calibration data, basal-1.0-4.5B auto-decided 58.6% of test decisions at 1.2% observed error (target 1%) vs 18.1% coverage for Jev under the same procedure, after per-decision-type calibration and on author-generated items whose test split was consulted during development (Abstract, Contributions, Limitations).

In a preregistered test on 1,500 ChaosNLI items, Jev's Choice ECE rose from 0.076 on the most-agreed quartile to 0.339 on the least-agreed (bias-corrected Delta 0.264 [0.244, 0.278]) with mean confidence 0.807 where 46.8% of annotators agreed; Noul degraded less (inconclusive), confidence still ranked contested items (AUROC 0.744), one temperature could not fix both strata, and Jev was far better calibrated than the local generative Qwen2.5-1.5B baseline (Abstract, Table 2, Sec. 7.5-7.8).

Because Jev stays confident on items where 100 annotators split (40% of hard items at confidence >= 0.9 with mean agreement 0.505), its probabilities do not estimate how many people would agree, which limits its use as a stand-in for population judgement (Abstract, Sec. 8).

On the open Kev-0.8B with four questions per call, the strongest planted note per item made at least one related answer wrong in 89% (77/87) of eligible action-gate items and two or more in 29%, and when it flipped allow/block the risk answer was also wrong 48.4% vs 8.4% (H1 supported in 3 of 4 pairs); all results are for Kev-0.8B, not Jev (Sec. 5.2, Sec. 6.2).

A coverage-matched gate (tau50) let none of 589 attack flips through, but a fixed 0.8 gate on raw scores passed 42, and notes agreeing with existing mistakes produced 14 oversight switch-offs per temperature that cleared both decision and review gates; a second call without the untrusted text caught all flips but none of these boosted mistakes (Sec. 5.3-5.5).

On 41 supplier-payment texts x 3 reruns (492 observations), open Laya was perfectly repeatable on identical inputs but meaning-preserving rewordings gave 32.38-56.67% pairwise decision disagreement, swapping Laya checkpoints changed 92.68%/78.05% of ternary decisions (36.59%/43.90% at the approve gate), and removing class definitions moved 19/41 typed-decisions outputs across the approve gate (Results).
